Not A without compiler, flags and CPU model.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Speed factor of the Holters-Parker resampler over libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST, from doc/speed_chart.png: 48k to 96k 39.8x, 96k to 48k 16.9x, 44.1k to 48k 21.2x, 48k to 44.1k 21.8x (doc/writeup.md: '10-40x faster'). Not quality-matched: the HP resampler runs a 4th-order IIR filter, libsamplerate SINC_FASTEST is a 97 dB SNR / 80% bandwidth sinc converter.
corrections.workload: One timed pass (std::chrono, no warm-up, no repeats) resampling a 1,000,000-sample 100 Hz float sine in 2048-sample blocks, mono, for four ratios (2.0, 0.5, 1.088, 0.919; the 44.1k/48k ratios are rounded), comparing the SSE-vectorised Holters-Parker multi-rate IIR resampler (src/HPResampler.h, src/src_utils/HPFilters.h) against libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST (src/LibSamplerRateSRC.h), harness src/src_test.cpp.
corrections.hardware: Linux machine with an Intel i7 CPU, model not stated (doc/writeup.md); the author also reports comparable results on a Mac and close to 40x on Windows, without numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version not stated. Documented build is 'cmake -Bbuild; cmake --build build --config Release'; on a single-config Linux generator '--config Release' is ignored and neither the top-level CMakeLists.txt nor the current libsamplerate and libsndfile CMakeLists.txt set a default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so the optimisation level of the measured build is unknown (possibly unoptimised). libsamplerate is built from the third_party/libsamplerate submodule with the same flags as the HP code.
corrections.caveats: The two sides do different work. The HP resampler uses one 4th-order analog filter (the JUNO-60 bucket-brigade filter poles and zeros from Holters and Parker's DAFx 2018 paper, per src/src_utils/HPFilters.h; the README and writeup call it a 4th-order Butterworth), while libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST is documented at 97 dB SNR and 80% bandwidth (docs/api_misc.md). The author's own quality plot doc/HP_compare.png shows HP output with spurious components up to about -47 dB against a roughly -10 dB fundamental, where libsamplerate's spectrum stays smooth (read from the plot), and doc/writeup.md says 'I'm primarily interested in speed rather than quality'. In src/HPResampler.h the filter cutoff is set to the input Nyquist (sample_rate*0.5) for every ratio, so for 96k to 48k the anti-aliasing cutoff (48 kHz) sits above the 24 kHz output Nyquist (derived from code reading). Timing is a single pass on a 100 Hz sine with no repeats; quality stats are computed in src_test.cpp but never printed. Compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated. The code uses SSE intrinsics (x86 only) and code from the GPL-3.0 Surge Synthesizer. Last commit 2021-07-12.

notes: The chart numbers match the record. The 10-40x figure is also in the in-repo doc/writeup.md, so the record's note that it appears only in a blocked blog is wrong. The measured code does much less filtering than the baseline (a 4th-order IIR against a 97 dB sinc converter), so this is a speed-for-quality trade, not like-for-like work. baseline_in_list is set to false because libsamplerate is not among the video-audio baselines (FFmpeg components, x264/x265, Opus). verify.py does not apply 'language' from corrections, so record it as a decision override.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party headline figures (300x vs pySoX, 4x vs librosa.load) with no benchmark code, corpus, machine or flags in the repo; the 2-5x SoxBindings figure comes from a third-party notebook (iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata, 6 stars) with no hardware stated, which is not a well-known independent suite. Tier stays C; the verdict is a downgrade because the README's 'even when only using one thread' framing is overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, under 'Even when only using one thread': processes audio up to 300x faster than pySoX for single transforms and 2-5x faster than SoxBindings (via iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata), and reads audio files up to 4x faster than librosa.load 'in many cases'. The cited SoxBindings notebook times six single effects on LJ Speech at 22.05 kHz: SoxBindings 73.1/130.8/38.1/38.6/76.7/105.2 s against pedalboard 11.6/26.3/10.9/10.8/32.2/20.9 s (Compressor, Chorus, HighpassFilter, LowpassFilter, Phaser, Reverb), i.e. 2.4-6.3x (derived from page data). But pedalboard ran with tf.data num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE while SoxBindings ran serially, and a single Pedalboard effect chain was slower than the SoxBindings chain (357.2 s vs 305.2 s, 0.85x, derived from page data); only splitting the chain into parallel tf.data stages won (82.1 s). PR #85 first claimed 'up to 20x faster than librosa.load in certain cases', later tempered; no method given.
corrections.baseline: pySoX (Python wrapper that runs the SoX command-line program), SoxBindings (Python bindings to libsox) and librosa.load (audio file reading)
corrections.caveats: First-party claims without benchmark code, corpus, machine or compiler in the repo; no FFmpeg, libsamplerate or resampling comparison anywhere in the README, so the video-audio category fit is weak (the baselines are Python audio-effect and file-loading wrappers, not FFmpeg, x264/x265 or Opus). The 300x figure against pySoX includes pySoX launching a SoX subprocess and file I/O per transform, so it mostly measures process overhead. The only public numbers behind the SoxBindings claim (iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata notebook) ran pedalboard multi-threaded via tf.data AUTOTUNE against serial SoxBindings, contradicting the README's 'even when only using one thread', compared SoX and JUCE effects at default parameters (different algorithms), and showed a single Pedalboard chain slower than SoxBindings (357.2 s vs 305.2 s). The librosa figure traces to PR #85 ('up to 20x... in certain cases', later tempered to 4x) with no method. The C++ core is a pybind11 extension module (C++17, -O3 release builds) and is not shipped as a standalone C++ library; C++ users would use JUCE directly. GPL-3.0, with JUCE, Rubber Band and LAME linked in under GPL terms.
corrections.language: Python (C++17 core on JUCE, pybind11 extension)

notes: The README compares pedalboard against pySoX, SoxBindings and librosa.load only, with no machine stated; the 300x and 4x figures are first-party, and the 2-5x figure is a small third-party notebook whose method contradicts the README's one-thread framing. Kept at C with the measured-work mismatch documented; the category fit to video-audio is loose. verify.py does not apply 'language' from corrections, so record it as a decision override.

tier_reason: The README Performance tables come from the public in-process harness benches/vs_libopus.rs against libopus 1.6.1 through the opus FFI crate, and the release profile is in Cargo.toml, but the CPU model, OS, rustc version and the system libopus build flags are not stated, so it is first-party C rather than A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (x realtime, one pinned core; ratio = ruopus/libopus): decode SILK WB 16 kb/s 2095x vs 1171x (1.79x), hybrid FB 32 kb/s 1199x vs 850x (1.41x), CELT FB 64 kb/s 1389x vs 1566x (0.89x, slower). Encode at matched complexity 0: 734x vs 740x (0.99x), 560x vs 562x (1.00x), 1088x vs 1092x (1.00x). Encode against libopus at complexity 10 (ruopus also set to 10): SILK WB 16 kb/s 703x vs 221x (3.18x), hybrid FB 32 kb/s 424x vs 193x (2.20x), CELT FB 64 kb/s 693x vs 432x (1.60x); ruopus's complexity-10 encoder omits delayed-decision NSQ and warped noise shaping, so these ratios compare unequal work.
corrections.workload: In-process mono 48 kHz Opus decode and encode of a 6 s synthetic speech/music-like signal (tones under a syllabic envelope plus light noise) in 20 ms frames, one core, reported as x realtime (benches/vs_libopus.rs, timed until each run exceeds about 0.4 s). Decode inputs are libopus-encoded VBR packets for SILK WB 16 kb/s (VoIP), hybrid FB 32 kb/s (VoIP) and CELT FB 64 kb/s (Audio); each repetition builds a new decoder or encoder on both sides.
corrections.caveats: Baseline is libopus itself (not another Rust port), linked via the opus 0.3 FFI crate against the system libopus (1.6.1 per the README); its build flags and SIMD dispatch are not stated, nor are the CPU model, OS or rustc version. Decode is comparable work, but output is not bit-exact PCM: the decoder passes all twelve RFC 8251 vectors at 99.2-100% on opus_compare with bit-exact per-packet final ranges, while PCM differs in float rounding (default spectrograms/rustfft MDCT backend). The encoder produces a different bitstream from libopus, and its quality is checked only by waveform SNR (examples/encoder_quality.rs; the CHANGELOG reports higher SNR than libopus), not a perceptual metric. At complexity 10, ruopus skips delayed-decision NSQ and warped noise shaping that libopus runs, so the 1.6-3.18x encode wins compare unequal work; at matched complexity 0, encode is at parity. In the encode bench, ruopus chooses its mode through encode_auto, while libopus gets an explicit application and VBR setting, and the bench does not check that both pick the same mode. CELT decode is slower than libopus. The signal is synthetic. The library is pure Rust with no C API (Python bindings via PyO3), so C++ use needs a custom FFI shim.
corrections.language: Rust (pure Rust, no FFI; Python bindings via PyO3)

notes: The README numbers match the record, and the bench code confirms that libopus 1.6.1 via FFI is the baseline, measured in-process on identical packets and input. The headline 3.18x encode figure compares ruopus at its fixed effort against libopus complexity 10; at matched complexity 0, encode is at parity. The decode wins (1.41-1.79x on SILK and hybrid) are like-for-like work. verify.py does not apply 'language' from corrections, so record it as a decision override.
